newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OPINION - Politics spice up E.Europe coffee sector.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Politics spice up E.Europe coffee sector.

text.p: By Hans de Heer, president of Swiss coffee firm Interlink SA
Since the opening of central and eastern European coffee markets, regular buying patterns could be observed.

In January the market is usually virtually dead as a result of previous heavy spending during the year-end festivities and, specially in Russia, many companies close until after the Orthodox Christmas and New Year around mid-January.
In February and March, business gradually picks up to reach full swing in April. Buying will then start to decline gradually until July and the summer period is traditionally very quiet.

Purchases rise substantially again in September, reaching a peak in November and December as hoarding ahead of the Christmas period resumes. These cycles were unchanged until end-1995. NEW BUYING PATTERNS EMERGE IN 1996

In early 1996, traders expected turnover to decline after heavy sales as a result of the traditional market influences. But for the first time since 1990, sales flourished in January and February in total contradiction to established patterns.
The strong pre-summer months turned out to be mediocre and the year-end buying rush never materialised.
The disruption of buying cycles, mainly in the former Soviet Republics and Balkan countries, shows these new markets are still very unstable and heavily dependent on political and economic factors.

A quick analysis shows that when the Russian Duma voted new credits to pay several months of overdue salaries in late 1995, the fresh buying power extended the traditional pre-Christmas business boom well beyond February 1996.
When the recent election period in Bulgaria resulted in hyper-inflation and a paralysed banking sector, coffee sales dropped instantaneously.
The government has changed, moving from left to right and the newly-elected president will have to stabilise the currency urgently in order to avoid a total collapse of the economy.

As the lev lost ground against the dollar to 510 from 200 in less than four months, with the average monthly salary at less than $30 and a retail coffee price of $4 per kg, Bulgarians found it hard to maintain their coffee drinking habits.

With the Romanian leu officially quoted against the dollar at 3,600 but the black market rate around 4,850 and banks selling their little dollar availabilities at that rate, and with almost all dollar payments suspended since the elections, coffee deliveries to roasters have come to a standstill.

And with Russian workers still waiting to receive their August and September salaries, there is no need to look further why pre-Christmas sales are so slow. IMPORT TAXES FAVOUR SMALL TO MEDIUM DOMESTIC ROASTERS

The majority of the small and medium-sized roasters continue to buy hand-to-mouth all year long. They can afford to do so in the countries mentioned as there is very little competition from larger roaster groups working in several month coverage.

Despite high taxation (around 120 percent in Romania, including excise tax and VAT, there are ways around this, for example Russia allows VAT exemptions for imports through special associations such as for Afganistan war veterans.
The substantial savings on taxes represent a comfortable cushion to absorb any competitive buying advantages which more sophisticated roasters might earn on their purchasing strategy.

Local roasters are more or less shielded from foreign competition. Pricing strategies for roasted coffee are non-existent and increases in green coffee prices and variations in exchange rates are immediately reflected in the final price.

With current inflation rates and salaries not rising at the same speed or simply not being paid, coffee is becoming more and more expensive. Imports in central and eastern European countries probably fell slightly in 1996 or at best stagnated. QUALITY GENERALLY MAINTAINED DESPITE INDUSTRY PROBLEMS

With all the problems encountered in these countries, it is surprising that quality standards have been maintained and that only very few roasters were tempted to add lower grade coffees to their blends.

In Russia the standard is set by the former state-owned factory which still dominates the roasted whole bean coffee segment and which uses only high quality arabicas in its famous 500-gram pack. Smaller companies try to compete with their own brand names, but still use the same quality beans.

Bulgaria and Romania are robusta countries. Some years ago black beans were part of some blends but this low grade seems to have disappeared and quality has improved in Romania as many blends already include a fair share of Brazil robustas.

Ukraine is probably the exception on quality. The private roasting industry has only started to develop seriously over the past two years and due to the domestic problems more roasters are adding lower grade coffees to their traditional 100 percent Colombian or Central Americans, to offer cheaper products. GROWTH POTENTIAL REMAINS DESPITE MEDICORE 1996
If 1996 was not a memorable year for coffee in Central and Eastern European countries and if hoped-for growth has come to a standstill, it does not mean that the potential has altered.

Many growth forecasts are simply based on the size of these markets without taking political and economic influences into consideration. This year has been a perfect example of the impact these forces can have on consumption.
In the Balkans, growth will no doubt resume in 1997 if new governments manage to stabilise the currencies and revise the system of taxes on coffee imports.
In Russia a certain drop in consumption in larger cities can easily be compensated by higher sales into more remote regions where distribution channels are not yet well established.

Many roasters active around cities have already started to develop contacts with regions where competition is less fierce. With new distribution channels reaching as-yet untouched areas, consumption throughout Russia should remain stable and most probably show interesting growth over the years to come.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as necessarily as representing the views of Reuters).
